posts.title: Why the CDO role keeps failing in Nigeria
posts.h1: Why the CDO role keeps failing in Nigeria.
posts.byline: By the Design Lever research team
posts.standfirst: The full-time Chief Design Officer is the right role at the wrong moment for most Nigerian growth-stage companies. The mandate is sound; the hire, at Series A to C, rarely survives contact with reality.

body.text: One pattern repeats across our interviews: companies hire a senior design leader before the organisation can hold one. No structure, no measurement culture, no peer at the table. Within eighteen months the leader leaves.
The tenure problem

A full-time CDO in Nigeria costs ₦25–60M in the first year once salary, recruitment and benefits are counted, and the statistical tenure is under two years. That is an expensive way to learn that the function was not ready.
The gap is never talent. It is the infrastructure the talent is dropped into.
The fractional window

The fractional model exists precisely for this window: build the leadership system, prove design on the P&L, and hand it over running, so that when the company does hire full-time, there is a seat worth taking.

posts.cardSummary: The full-time hire is right in theory and wrong at your stage. A look at the tenure data.

posts.title: What a design health assessment actually finds
posts.h1: What a design health assessment actually finds.
posts.byline: By the Design Lever research team
posts.standfirst: Five costs show up in almost every leaderless design function. None of them appear on a design budget line.

body.text: Rework, duplicated tooling, stalled approvals, quiet attrition, and brand drift. Each is measurable, and each traces back to the same missing role.
The five costs
Engineering rework alone typically runs 15–30% of build time in functions without design leadership. The others compound it.
The costs are real and recurring. They are just filed under other departments.
What to do with the findings
Score the function, price the leaks, and decide: hire, contract, or install fractional leadership until the organisation is ready.

posts.cardSummary: The five costs that show up in almost every leaderless design function.

posts.title: Design on the P&L, in Nigeria
posts.h1: Design on the P&L, in Nigeria.
posts.byline: By the Design Lever research team
posts.standfirst: A design function is defensible when it is tied to numbers a board already reads. Everything else is decoration.

body.text: Revenue per release, conversion, support-ticket volume, rework hours. Pick two, baseline them, and report movement quarterly.
Choosing the numbers
The metric must belong to the business, not to design. NPS is weaker than repeat purchase. Usability scores are weaker than support cost.
Design budgets survive planning season when they arrive attached to a P&L line.
Reporting rhythm
One page, once a quarter, same format every time. The discipline is the credibility.

posts.cardSummary: How to make a design function defensible to a board that only reads numbers.

posts.title: The eighteen-month exit curve
posts.byline: By the Design Lever research team
posts.standfirst: Senior designers do not leave for money first. They leave when the ceiling is structural.

body.text: Across our interviews the exits cluster at month fourteen to twenty. The pattern is consistent: no leadership path, no measurement culture, no advocate at the table.
What moves the curve
A named design owner, a visible growth path, and work tied to business outcomes. Teams with all three retain seniors past three years.
The exit curve is a leadership artefact, not a loyalty problem.
The cost of the curve
Replacing a senior designer costs six to nine months of salary in recruitment, ramp and lost velocity. Retention is the cheapest design investment available.

posts.cardSummary: Why senior designers leave, and the leadership factors that move the curve.

posts.title: A CDO who stayed back home
posts.h1: A CDO who stayed back home.
posts.byline: By the Design Lever research team
posts.standfirst: Most senior design leaders leave. This one stayed past the two-year mark, and the difference was structural.

body.text: The company gave design a seat, a budget, and a number to own before the hire was made. The role had a floor to stand on from day one.
What the company did
An executive sponsor, a measurement baseline, and a mandate written into the operating plan. None of it was expensive. All of it was rare.
I stayed because the job was real. The title was the least of it.
What other companies can copy
Build the seat before the hire. If the seat cannot be built yet, contract the leadership until it can.

posts.cardSummary: Structured conversations on how design investment performs inside the business.

posts.title: Investing before the case studies
posts.byline: By the Design Lever research team
posts.standfirst: There was no African benchmark to point to. This founder invested in design leadership anyway.

body.text: The bet: if design decisions kept reaching the CEO desk, the company was paying an executive salary for design leadership already, just badly.
The decision
A fractional design executive, one day a week, owning quality disputes and the hiring bar. The CEO desk cleared within a quarter.
We were paying for design leadership either way. We chose to pay for the real thing.
The result
Release rework fell, senior designers stopped leaving, and the first full-time design hire landed into a working system.

posts.cardSummary: Recurring data on compensation, seniority, career progression and leadership access.

posts.title: Leading from abroad
posts.byline: By the Design Lever research team
posts.standfirst: Japa took the designer. It did not have to take the leadership.

body.text: A London-based African design director kept a standing fractional engagement with a Lagos scale-up: two days a month on site, weekly leadership cover remote.
How the model works
Timezone-adjacent, culturally fluent, and senior. The diaspora bench is a leadership asset the continent has barely priced.
Leaving the country does not mean leaving the work.
What it takes
A clear mandate, a local deputy, and honest scoping. The model fails only when it is treated as advisory instead of accountable.

posts.cardSummary: Approved and anonymised baseline and outcome metrics from Practice engagements.

posts.title: From bottleneck to pace-setter
posts.byline: By the Design Lever research team
posts.standfirst: One quarter after installing design leadership, the slowest function in the company set the release pace.

body.text: The team was talented and stuck: approvals queued at the founder, a design system existed in name only, and every release relitigated the basics.
The install
A fractional design executive took the approval queue, shipped the design system, and set a weekly critique with seniors in the room.
Nothing about the team changed. Everything about the system did.
The numbers
Release cycle time fell 40% in the first quarter. Design-caused rework halved. The function now briefs the roadmap instead of receiving it.

posts.cardSummary: A health-tech team on the quarter their design function changed gear.
